主要内容: On December 3, 2018, Craig Phillips, Counselor to the Secretary, delivered remarks on the evolving structure of the U.S. Treasury market. The remarks were prepared for delivery at the Fourth Annual Conference on the Evolving Structure of the U.S. Treasury Market. Phillips highlighted the importance of Treasury securities transaction data collected by the Financial Industry Regulatory Authority (FINRA) through its Trade Reporting and Compliance Engine (TRACE). He discussed the significance of this data for the Treasury as an issuer and for the regulatory community. Phillips also outlined suggestions for improving the data to better reflect the unique aspects of the Treasury market. He emphasized the importance of ensuring the data is clear, complete, and useful for understanding the impact of public dissemination on market structure and liquidity. The remarks underscored the commitment to working with FINRA and the Interagency Working Group (IAWG) to enhance the TRACE data and support the efficient functioning of the Treasury market. Phillips also emphasized the importance of maintaining a robust and liquid Treasury market. He highlighted that reducing debt service costs could lead to lower benchmark rates for corporate, agency, and mortgage instruments, offering cost benefits to borrowers. A liquid Treasury market also provides significant advantages for market participants using Treasury securities for hedging or as collateral. The Treasury’s guiding principles include 'doing no harm' to the market and considering the interests of all investors to encourage a broad investor base. These principles remain central to the Treasury’s approach to market structure and innovation. The discussion also included an analysis of transaction volumes, trade sizes, and market segments such as the dealer-to-customer (DtC) and interdealer broker (IDB) markets. The data revealed that average daily transaction volumes were nearly $600 billion, with the DtC and IDB markets being the primary contributors. The Treasury also examined trade size distributions for nominal coupons and other securities, noting differences in trading patterns across on- and off-the-run securities.
